cues.text: Let us now turn to Chapter 9, an independent practice case on workplace monitoring.
This is a revision exercise.
It asks you to apply what you have learned, so I will walk through the scenario and then through the analysis the source expects from you.
Here is the first scenario.
A fictional logistics company proposes installing monitoring software that records employees' screens at all times, including during breaks, in order to detect fraud.
Notice the three features of this proposal: the recording is continuous, it covers every employee, and it continues during breaks.
The stated aim is fraud detection.
Now notice the alternative the source offers.
The company could instead limit access logs to sensitive transactions, and investigate specific anomalies under a controlled policy.
So you have two designs.
One watches everything, all the time.
The other records access to sensitive transactions only, and investigates only when something specific looks wrong.
The source then tells you what to analyse.
Start with the stakeholders.
There are four: employees, customers, the employer, and security staff.
Ask what each one needs.
Employees have an interest in privacy and dignity at work.
Customers have an interest in not being defrauded and in their data being handled safely.
The employer has an interest in protecting its business.
Security staff operate the system, and they carry responsibility for how it is used.
Next, the source asks you to consider the legitimate fraud-prevention goal.
Fraud prevention is a real and legitimate aim, so you should not dismiss it.
The ethical question is whether this particular means is justified.
Then examine the scope of surveillance.
What exactly is recorded, when, and for how long?
Recording screens at all times, including breaks, is very broad.
Closely linked is the idea of reasonable expectations.
During a break, what would an employee reasonably expect?
Most people would expect a degree of personal space, so recording at that time is hard to defend.
Now consider autonomy, which is the employee's capacity to make their own choices and to act without constant observation.
Then proportionality.
This asks whether the intrusion is in balance with the goal, and whether a less intrusive method could achieve the same purpose.
This is exactly where the alternative matters.
Limited logging of sensitive transactions is narrower than continuous recording.
The source also lists data security.
Recordings of screens may capture personal messages, passwords or private information, so they must be protected.
Then the employment power imbalance: an employee is dependent on the employer for their livelihood.
And finally accountability, meaning who answers for how the system is used, and how misuse is detected and corrected.
The source then asks you to compare three approaches: narrower logging, targeted investigations, and continuous monitoring.
Narrower logging records only access to sensitive transactions.
Targeted investigations are triggered by a specific anomaly and are limited to it.
Continuous monitoring records everything about everyone.
As you compare them, weigh effectiveness against intrusion, and ask which one best respects proportionality.
Now, what must a reasoned recommendation contain?
The source says it must define six things.
First, notice: how employees are told about the monitoring.
Second, access restrictions: who may see the data.
Third, retention: how long data is kept.
Fourth, oversight: who supervises the system.
Fifth, a complaint process: how employees can challenge or report concerns.
Sixth, measurement of effectiveness: how the company will know whether the measure actually reduces fraud.
If your recommendation lacks any of these six, it is incomplete.
The source adds two further considerations.
Consider potential retaliation, where monitoring data might be used to punish employees for unrelated reasons or for raising concerns.
And consider chilling effects, where people change their behaviour, speak less freely or hold back legitimate activity because they feel watched.
Finally, there are two warnings.
Do not assume consent resolves the imbalance.
Because of the power imbalance, an employee's agreement may not be freely given.
And do not assume that every employee is a suspect.
Blanket monitoring treats everyone as presumed guilty, which conflicts with fair treatment.
Now the second scenario.
A photo-sharing service begins inferring sensitive interests from image metadata, and shares the resulting profiles with advertisers.
You are asked to do four things.
First, distinguish the original purpose from the secondary profiling.
Users shared photos to store or share them.
Inferring sensitive interests and passing profiles to advertisers is a different, secondary use.
Second, assess the lawful basis and meaningful controls.
Ask what justification the service has for this new use, and whether users have real, usable control over it.
Third, examine metadata risks.
Metadata is data about the photo, and it can reveal more than users realise.
Fourth, propose privacy-preserving alternatives, meaning ways to pursue the service's goals with less exposure of personal information.
Finally, a clear note on status.
These are independent revision exercises.
Neither is a response to the graded final case.
So use them to practise, not as the answer to your assessed work.

To consolidate for the exam, review these topics: contextual privacy, metadata, active and passive data, consent fatigue, fingerprinting, profiling, surveillance types, proportionality, chilling effect, platform responsibilities, user rights, and ethical design.
When you attempt the exercises, try to bring as many of these as you can into your reasoning.
